newsitem.title: USA: Sun Microsystems to Unveil JavaChip.
newsitem.headline: Sun Microsystems to Unveil JavaChip.

text.p: Sun Microsystems Inc will unveil on Friday technical details about a new computer chip that's designed to let consumer electronic devices -- everything from handheld computers to cellular telephones -- tap into the Internet.

Sun, a maker of high-end computers for managing the flow of information through networks, will release the specifications of the JavaChip. The chip will be based on Java, a computer language that specializes in letting a wide range of computers share information with each other through networks.

Sun released a sketch of its plans for a network- specialized microprocessor earlier this year. The Sunnyvale, California-based company is looking for ways to embed Java into almost every kind of computer -- from personal computers to telephones -- that can be hooked up to the global communication networks.

The JavaChip can be used in cellular telephones, for example, to let people read their email, or to look up phone numbers on online directories, said Chet Silvestri, president of Sun Microelectronics, the arm that designs chips.

As consumer electronics "become more network-oriented, you'll need more performance" from the devices' brains, Silvestri said. "The amount of information that you are going to want to load and process is going to go up dramatically."
The microprocessor currently in the typical cellular phone, however, doesn't have enough processing power to handle anything beyond displaying digits dialed, or remembering speed-dial numbers.

Sun is trying to sell the JavaChip to several companies designing so-called network computers, handheld personal digital assistants and other communication devices. So far, Japan's NEC Corp., Mitsubishi Electronics and Korea's Samsung Corp. are interested in the technology, Sun said.

Silvestri said it's too early to tell how much revenue the JavaChip could bring in for Sun. Sample batches of the chip will be sold to manufacturers in the middle of 1997, with the first products coming out late next year or early 1998.
